title: The Zcash Brief - Wednesday, September 2, 2026
content:
Now I have enough information to compile the digest. Let me synthesize the key active threads from the last 24 hours and recent days into the editorial briefing format.

The Zcash Brief - Wednesday, September 2, 2026

Zcash finds itself at a constitutional moment: the ballots are open, the clock is ticking, and the soul of NU7 hangs in the balance.

THE BIG STORIES

  • NU7 Coinholder Vote - Valar Group and Project Tachyon launched a coinholder vote on August 25, running approximately 18 days, to decide the scope of NU7 — the vote that was once cancelled in the chaos of the Orchard counterfeiting bug. The stakes are enormous: coinholders will decide whether Zcash should replace traditional halvings with a smoother issuance curve under the Network Sustainability Mechanism, when fee reissuance begins, whether to deprecate the legacy Sprout transaction format, and whether to slash block times from 75 seconds to 25. If participation falls below the 1 million ZEC threshold, the outcome will not be considered representative of the broader coinholder community — meaning a low-turnout result could be dismissed entirely, and the governance limbo would deepen.
  • ZCAP Poll Now Open: NU7 (August 2026) - Running concurrently with the coinholder vote, the Zcash Foundation opened a SIV poll of the Zcash Community Advisory Panel (ZCAP), running until Monday, September 14th at 19:00 UTC, with the explicit purpose of resolving outstanding scope questions for NU7. The dual-track structure — coinholders voting in parallel with the advisory panel — is itself a governance experiment, and community voices have been sharp on the question of whether a coinholder poll constitutes a binding "vote" at all. One prominent forum contributor argued pointedly that there is no ZIP that approves making Zcash protocol decisions by vote or that specifies how to do so — a constitutional objection that hangs unresolved over the entire exercise.
  • Global Ambassador Elzz August 2026 Report - Filed just hours ago, this month's ambassador report from Nigeria signals that Zcash's grassroots outreach machinery is grinding forward even as protocol debates rage above it. In August, Ambassador Elzz focused on Zcash onboarding, education, and ecosystem participation, with the flagship initiative being Proof of Privacy — #ZcashClass26, an online onboarding and education campaign designed to create a more participatory path into the Zcash ecosystem through community-led recruitment, live education, and gamification. Whether this kind of bottom-up momentum can translate into voter turnout for the NU7 coinholder poll — and push it past the critical 1 million ZEC threshold — is the question nobody is saying aloud but everyone is thinking.
  • Community Feature Wishlist: A Thread - Surfaced two days ago, this open-ended forum thread invites anyone — community members, moderators, even developers — to dream publicly about features they want to see in the Zcash ecosystem. The thread is explicitly designed for community members, moderators, and developers to post potential features they wish to see in the Zcash ecosystem, and for people who can work on them to pick them up. It arrives at a charged moment: with NU7's scope being litigated through formal votes, this informal wishlist thread is a reminder that Zcash's community still has ideas that may not fit neatly into any upgrade cycle — and that the gap between governance and inspiration remains very much open.

THE PULSE

The forum is operating on two speeds simultaneously this week. At the top, a high-stakes governance drama is playing out with near-constitutional gravity — a coinholder vote and a ZCAP poll running in tandem, both chasing a September 14th deadline, both carrying the unresolved question of whether any of this is actually binding. The mechanics are novel: a voting round includes a "snapshot height," an "end time," and multiple proposals, with one Ironwood ZEC at snapshot height equaling one vote — a coin-weighted democracy that is elegant in theory and deeply contested in practice. Meanwhile, the community's builders and ambassadors are quietly doing the unglamorous work of onboarding users in Nigeria, dreaming up feature wishlists, and shipping engineering updates — as if the protocol's future were already settled. It isn't.

WATCH LIST

  • The Coinholder Voting Chain - This technical deep-dive thread explains the infrastructure beneath the NU7 vote itself, and it deserves close attention from anyone who wants to understand whether the results will hold up to scrutiny. This post includes details of the voting chain being used in the latest NU7 coinholder vote, intended for the pre-security incident vote. A distributed election authority made up of at least 10 validators counts votes without ever learning who cast them, with the shielded design keeping voter privacy intact while still producing a tally anyone can verify — a cryptographic promise that will be tested in real time as the September deadline approaches.
  • ZF Engineering Update – 10th to 23rd August 2026 - The Zcash Foundation's latest engineering dispatch reveals a protocol that is quietly maturing beneath the governance noise. Zebra 6.3.0 was published as a recommended security release, with a notable new capability merged: Zebra can now serve light wallets directly, without a separate lightwalletd server sitting in between. Engineers also published a guide for zcashd operators moving to Zebra, and began early work on a faster way for nodes to connect to each other — infrastructure investments that will matter enormously when NU7 finally lands, whatever its eventual scope turns out to be.

ZEC crossed $1,000 last week for the first time in nearly a decade, hit $1,249 on Saturday, and the privacy sector is now the only crypto category trading above its level at Bitcoin's October 2025 peak. A 2,496% rally driven by the Grayscale ETF and the SEC closing its investigation without action. The price is screaming. But the forum? The forum is having a completely different conversation.

Someone posted "What Is Stopping Zcash From Reaching More People?" — and the replies are more revealing than the question. Another says people know about Zcash, they just don't think privacy matters. A mother says her daughters now send her ZEC for Mother's Day. Three completely different realities of the same ecosystem, sitting in the same thread. The gap between price action and lived usability has never been more visible.

Meanwhile, a thread called "Proof of Work Must Never Be Abandoned" is making a case most people aren't engaging with yet: that privacy isn't Zcash's soul — PoW is, and stripping it would reduce ZEC to just another replicable token. The counterargument is Ethereum — $100B in staked capital, thriving without mining. Neither side is wrong, which is what makes it worth reading.

The builder activity is real right now. ZecScope wants to build a public ZIP and upgrade tracker. A Flutter wallet SDK, a pure-JS Zcash library, and a mixnet proxy for light wallets all surfaced in the last 48 hours. Whether this wave of tooling sustains or fades with the grant cycle is worth watching honestly.

The NU7 coinholder vote closes in six days. 3.35 million ZEC in. The questions on the ballot — issuance curves, block times, Sprout deprecation — will define what Zcash actually becomes next. The ZCAP poll closes September 14th alongside it.

The grant application I keep coming back to this week is the Security Audit of Zaino, submitted by Cyfrin-Mark just over a week ago — and I think it deserves a real spotlight rather than a bullet point. The proposal is for an independent security audit of Zaino, the Rust-based indexer built by Zingolabs as part of the Z3 stack. Zaino sits between Zebra and every wallet or light client that depends on it — but unlike zcashd, Zebra, and librustzcash (which have audit histories from NCC Group, Least Authority, and Trail of Bits), Zaino hasn't had a published third-party security audit. That's a real gap. Zaino is now load-bearing infrastructure for the entire post-zcashd ecosystem, and its attack surface is nontrivial: it's also in the middle of significant internal modularization, with individual indexes becoming configurable and opt-in so operators can build only the indexes they need. The timing of this audit proposal — right when Zaino is being rearchitected — is either perfect or slightly awkward depending on how you think about auditing moving targets. I lean toward perfect: better to audit a design in motion than to wait until it's calcified and something goes wrong. The question ZCG should be asking isn't just whether to fund this, but whether the scope covers the new modular architecture specifically.


What gives this audit proposal additional urgency is what came out of the September 3rd Arborist Call, which was dense with infrastructure news. The Zebra team completed a major refactor of its transaction types — replacing Zebra's duplicated transaction representation with a wrapper around the upstream zcash_primitives type. The change touched more than 5,000 lines of code and removes duplicated transaction logic, clearing the way for further integration work. Meanwhile in librustzcash, PR #3022 merged decryption using ZIP 316 outgoing viewing keys, and PR #2992 is in review for detecting transparent spends when scanning full blocks — which matters for anyone building wallet-level transparent spend detection without a trusted server. ZIP 316 Revision 2 implementation is also nearly ready to land. A lot of load-bearing code is in motion all at once.


The conversation I most want to see happen publicly right now is the fee debate that's been fermenting since the September 3rd call. ZIP editors are considering a Shielded Labs proposal to reduce the marginal ZIP 317 fee to 1,000 zatoshis per logical action. That's the simple part. The interesting part is what Kris raised on top of it: potentially removing ZIP editors from routine fee adjustments entirely, and using historical ZEC/USD price data to calculate a minimum fee denominated in USD — an idea that would let fees respond systematically to ZEC's market price rather than requiring repeated manual tweaks. Pili expressed reservations about anchoring fees to USD, Zooko suggested testing competing approaches and potentially seeking independent economic analysis, and no decision was reached. I find myself genuinely torn. Anchoring to USD introduces an oracle dependency and a philosophical tension — Zcash fees denominated in a surveillance currency feels ironic. But leaving fees as a manual ZIP-editor decision at ZEC $1,200 creates real friction: a user with 270,000 tiny transparent UTXOs literally cannot shield them because the fee would be 13.5 ZEC. Now may be the time to act on dynamic fees given the rising price, adoption, and attention. That's not a theoretical edge case at current prices — that's a real person unable to self-custody. The Arborist Call surfaced the tension but didn't resolve it. That resolution should probably happen somewhere more visible than a bi-weekly dev call.


One more small thing from the grant board that I think is underrated: the Zcash Privacy Literacy Lab Canada, posted last week. It's a $15,000 ZCG application to build a free, account-free learning module with 12 documented scenarios showing what shielded transactions actually protect. Twelve concrete scenarios. No login required. In a moment when ZEC is above $1,000 and curious newcomers are arriving from ETF press coverage with no mental model of what shielded even means — this is exactly the kind of unglamorous infrastructure that pays off. I hope it doesn't get lost in the shuffle next to the larger, louder proposals.

Let me tell you about a grant that almost didn't happen — and what the fight to get it approved reveals about how Zcash decides who deserves to build in the ecosystem. The Zcash Arabia (August to December 2026) application is, on its surface, a regional community outreach grant. Arabic-language Zcash content, IRL events, community building in the MENA region. Standard stuff. But buried in the paper trail is something worth slowing down for. ZCG gave the original Zcash Arabia proposal a unanimous rejection in March 2025. They came back. By February 2026 they got unanimous approval on a Q1 2026 application. Then came the rejections again — the committee's rejection of their June-to-September 2026 proposal was mainly due to concerns about limited community engagement and the lack of IRL events. So what did the team do? They organized IRL events. They adapted. They filed again. And at the August 31 ZCG meeting, it passed — but not unanimously. Two committee members, Zerodartz and Artkor, voted against it. A slim majority carried it through. ZCG confirmed on the forum: "ZArabia at the most recent meeting, ZCG voted to approve this proposal."


Here's what I keep turning over in my head: what does it actually take to prove community legitimacy to ZCG? The Zcash Arabia team pointed out in their August application that the committee had "largely overlooked the positive results" achieved online, while roughly 80% of other funded community initiatives conduct their work online, with only about 20% consisting of IRL events. That's a fair shot. And it landed — eventually. But the question it raises is uncomfortable: if online community-building is already recognized and funded by ZCG for other grantees, why did Zcash Arabia have to fight through five-plus application cycles to get there? There's no clean answer. Maybe the committee is appropriately skeptical of new regional grants until they prove staying power. Maybe there's a consistency problem in how standards are applied. Probably both things are true at once. What I find genuinely interesting is that a team getting rejected again and again — by a unanimous vote — didn't give up, kept iterating, and eventually forced a decision. That takes something. Whether you think the outcome was deserved or not, the persistence itself is worth acknowledging.


While that drama played out in the grants forum, something quieter but maybe more consequential landed in librustzcash this week. Two separate PRs merged in short succession: PR #3024, fixing a zcashd HD path regex, was pushed by daira, and PR #2998 addressed a wallet migration failure on UIVK-only accounts. That second one matters more than it sounds. With zcashd having reached its final End-of-Support halt on July 18th at block height 3,417,100, every user still on zcashd needs to migrate their wallet. A silent failure on UIVK-only accounts during migration isn't a footnote — it's the kind of bug that strands people. Getting it fixed and merged this week is exactly the kind of unglamorous, load-bearing work that the post-zcashd transition depends on.


And then there's this, which genuinely caught me off guard. The Zakura team — which is Valar Group and Project Tachyon's node implementation — published a series of cryptographic optimization write-ups last month. The headline number: they adapted libsecp256k1's modular inversion to the Pasta curves and improved performance by 4.6x, and have also been working on faster Ironwood Merkle hashing from position-weighted Sinsemilla. Now, work is underway to upstream or backport those performance improvements from Valar Group's forks into the Zcash core libraries, with Danny Williams leading the effort and several pasta_curves pull requests currently seeking additional review. A 4.6x speed improvement on core curve arithmetic isn't something you just file away. That could meaningfully affect proof generation times and eventually wallet sync — things that directly touch real users. The fact that these gains are being actively shepherded back into the canonical repos rather than staying siloed in a fork is the part I want to see more of. Ecosystem wins only count if they compound.

The NU7 vote closes in 72 hours — and the part that keeps slipping past the eligibility debates and wallet support threads: this poll is advisory. Full stop. Anyone is free to carry out a poll. Calling it a 'vote' misleads about its force." So what happens Monday when the results land? Developers read them. And then — what exactly? There's no ZIP compelling ECC or the Foundation or Valar Group to honor any particular outcome. The whole exercise runs on social trust, not code. That's the actual situation. And with $600M+ in ETF AUM now watching from the sidelines, social trust feels like a thinner foundation than the moment deserves.


Speaking of that ETF: as of September 10, ZCSH reported assets under management of $628.3 million and 6,979,300 shares outstanding. The number keeps climbing. But there's a structural tension underneath that deserves more airtime. The fund holds transparent ZEC for regulators, while roughly 90% of non-custodial Zcash activity is now invisible to chain-surveillance firms. So what exactly are ZCSH investors buying? Price exposure to a network whose core utility they cannot access through the product they own. A 2.5% fee leaks performance against holding coins in cold storage. Shielded pool usage, not the ticker, is the privacy product — an ETF that holds custody at Coinbase does not put those coins in a z-address. MEXC's analysts noted that a single product priced at ten times the going rate for a Bitcoin ETF invites a competitor, and a cheaper alternative would do more for Zcash liquidity than the original listing. Watch for a second-mover filing. It might matter more than the NU7 vote.


On-chain, the shielded pool numbers deserve a second look — not for what they show, but for what they might be hiding. As of September 3, 28.8% of all ZEC — 4,878,432 ZEC — sits in shielded pools, versus 7.6% five years ago and 23.1% a year ago. Real adoption momentum. But the vote eligibility rules mean that only spendable, shielded ZEC held in the Ironwood pool at the snapshot block height was eligible — which structurally excludes the enormous pile of ZEC sitting in ZCSH's transparent Coinbase custody addresses. The fund's ~387,000+ ZEC has no vote. The institutions who moved in at $1,000+ have no vote. So we have a poll of long-term self-custodying Zcashers deciding the protocol direction of a network that now has a nine-figure institutional audience watching from transparent wallets — no eligibility, no snapshot, no ballot. I don't know if that's a problem. But it feels like a question worth sitting with before Monday's results arrive.


And then today happened. ZEC tumbled Friday, briefly dipping below $1,100 amid a crypto market downturn sparked by hotter-than-expected U.S. producer price index data. Lookonchain flagged two large ZEC long positions fully liquidated for a combined 3,848.5 ZEC (~$4.33 million). The pullback was macro-triggered, not Zcash-specific — but it lands at an interesting moment. ZEC went from $42 a year ago to $1,294 on September 9. The $2.4B derivatives book is signaling what some are calling a potential liquidation trap. The community spent the week debating issuance curves and block times while leverage was quietly building in the background. The vote closes in three days. The NU7 implementation target is nineteen days after that. And today, the market reminded everyone that external forces don't care about your governance timeline.


And then there's the thread the community is rightfully dragging me for not covering: Private Money in the Sky. strahncryptography posted a proposal to broadcast Zcash blocks from a constellation of CubeSats in low earth orbit — one-way satellite downlink, no internet connection required, receive transactions via a dish on your roof. Demo constellation: ~$800K. Full network: $8-15M via SpaceX rideshare. The punchline is that it's not actually crazy. Blockstream has been doing Bitcoin satellite broadcasts since 2017. The difference is Zcash's shielded transactions mean the data coming down from orbit is actually private — you're not just censorship-resistant, you're surveillance-resistant. As illinoizzzec put it: "What is the KYC regime in low earth orbit?" The community lockbox sitting at $250-300M makes the price tag look like a rounding error. I genuinely don't know if this is visionary or unhinged, but in Zcash those two things have a habit of being the same thing.

title: The Zcash Daily - Friday, September 11, 2026

🛡️ The Zcash Daily — Friday, September 11, 2026


Here's the thing nobody is naming clearly enough: the Zcash rally isn't really a Zcash story — it's a regulatory-tolerance story. More than 335 days after Bitcoin's October 2025 all-time high, the privacy coin sector is the only crypto category trading above its level at that peak, up 213%, according to Glassnode data as of September 6. But zoom in and the picture gets narrower. The gain is concentrated in Zcash rather than spread across the sector, and as one analysis put it bluntly, "The trade that worked in 2026 was not 'privacy.' It was the privacy asset that regulators would tolerate and an ETF could hold." That's a more fragile thesis than the headline numbers suggest. Monero has privacy that's arguably stronger — default, not optional — but it's the harder asset to list on a regulated venue because it hides sender, receiver and amount on every transaction. Zcash gets the ETF. Monero doesn't. The community is celebrating the win without fully sitting with the reason for it.


And that ETF just unlocked another layer of leverage on top of the leverage already present in the futures market. ZCSH options trading launched on NYSE Arca on September 8 — and ZCSH remains the only exchange-traded product in the world offering spot exposure to ZEC. Options on top of a spot ETF on top of a $2.1 billion open interest futures book. The pullback today triggered roughly $27.6 million in ZEC futures liquidations over 24 hours, while futures volume remained exceptionally high near $8.3 billion, compared with roughly $760 million in spot volume. That ratio — more than ten times as much derivatives activity as spot — is the number I keep staring at. The community is debating issuance curves and block times while the derivatives tail is quietly getting large enough to wag the dog. ZEC dipped below $1,055 Friday after higher-than-expected U.S. inflation data sparked a crypto selloff — not a Zcash-specific event, just the market reminding everyone that narrative doesn't insulate price from macro.


Meanwhile, the conversation that deserves more oxygen than it's getting happened quietly at the September 3 Arborist Call. The ZIP editors are considering a Shielded Labs proposal to reduce the marginal ZIP 317 fee to 1,000 zatoshis per logical action. That's a meaningful reduction on its own. But the more interesting thing is what happened next: Kris proposed potentially removing ZIP editors from routine fee adjustments and using historical ZEC/USD price data to calculate a minimum fee denominated in USD — allowing fees to respond systematically to changes in ZEC's market price rather than requiring repeated manual adjustments. Pili expressed reservations about anchoring transaction fees to USD, while Zooko suggested continuing the discussion separately and potentially seeking independent economic analysis. No decision was reached, and the fee mechanism remains under discussion. But this is the actual design tension: ZEC at $1,100 means the current fee structure already costs users far more in real terms than it did at $42. A fee denominated in zatoshis doesn't care about price discovery. A fee denominated in USD is easier to reason about for users but introduces an oracle dependency into the protocol. I don't know which approach is right. I'm not sure anyone does yet.


The thing that got genuinely underreported this week — lost in the governance noise — is Zakura Common. Zakura released an open-source cryptography toolkit on August 29 that reduced private Zcash transaction construction from more than three seconds to below 200 milliseconds in some benchmark tests. The libraries speed mobile proof generation more than 14x, desktop more than 5x, Sinsemilla hashing more than 21x and zk-SNARK verification 4–8x. And the critical part: the improvements do not require an upgrade to Zcash itself. Wallet developers can ship this now. Zakura has moved to the new stack in version 1.3.0, and Vizor Wallet is among the first to integrate it. This is the kind of quiet, compounding infrastructure work that doesn't generate governance drama — but it's closer to the actual "why would someone use Zcash daily" question than anything on the NU7 ballot. A transaction that feels instant on your phone changes user behavior in ways that a halving-curve vote simply does not.


The NU7 poll closes Sunday and there's one data point worth holding alongside the result: the coinholder poll had 7.25% participation of circulating ZEC, and ballot counts varied significantly across questions — from 210 ballots on Tachyon down to 55 on Consensus Accounts. Fifty-five ballots on a question affecting a network now worth $18 billion. Project Tachyon received universal or near-universal support across every polling group — the most unambiguous signal from the entire poll. That's useful information. But 7.25% participation, with results spread unevenly across questions, is the community telling you something about its own attention span — or maybe about how hard it still is to actually move ZEC into a shielded wallet and cast a ballot. The friction of participating in Zcash governance is itself a governance problem, and nobody has filed a ZIP for it.
